patch.value:
## Problem
Only pm context and pm next are token-budget aware. Every other command — list, search, get, deps, graph, history, activity, validate, stats — can emit output proportional to workspace size. In a million-item workspace a single unqualified call can consume an agent's entire context window, and the agent has no way to know the ceiling in advance.

## Approach
Promote the budget concept from one command to the contract layer. Each command declares a budget; the shared packer degrades output when the budget would be exceeded; the envelope discloses the degradation so agents can decide whether to page for more.

## Relationship to shipped work
The token-budget context packer shipped the degradation ladder and completeness accounting. The token-cost regression gate shipped the corpus measurement. This item generalises both to the whole surface; it must reuse those implementations rather than fork them.

## Boundary
Not a rendering redesign — output format grammar stays with the uniform output contract work. Not relevance scoring — selection quality stays with the context relevance engine.
Contract-declared output token budgets: every command declares a default ceiling and degrades deterministically instead of emitting unbounded output

The contract table declares a default output token budget per command and per output format, generated rather than hand-maintained; Commands exceeding their budget apply the shared degradation ladder (projection narrowing, then bounded truncation) and disclose what was dropped in the envelope; A budget override flag and a no-budget escape hatch exist for human and pipeline use, and are documented as non-default; The token-cost corpus gate is extended to assert every command against its declared budget, failing on regression; Degradation never changes machine-readable field names or breaks the scripting contract
No pm invocation can blow an agent context window, and the degradation that prevented it is disclosed in the envelope

Token cost is the real currency of an agent-facing CLI. Today only the context assembler is budget-aware; every other command can return an arbitrarily large payload that an agent must pay for and then discard.
Makes token cost a declared, reviewable property of the command surface rather than an emergent property of workspace size.
Each command in the contract table carries a default token budget; exceeding it degrades projection or truncates with disclosure, never silently.

The token-cost regression gate and the context packer both shipped, so the measurement harness and the degradation ladder already exist. Generalising them across the surface is the remaining step, and it is cheapest before the grammar freeze fixes the command table.

Output-cost baseline measured 2026-07-25 against the shipped build (2026.7.25, 2,022-item workspace). Bytes of stdout, TOON default versus --json versus --json --lean:

| command | TOON | JSON | JSON+lean |
|---|---|---|---|
| context --limit 10 | 8,194 | 11,229 | 9,674 |
| next | 11,632 | 15,464 | 13,871 |
| list --limit 20 | 3,912 | 4,693 | 4,666 |
| get <id> | 7,349 | 8,294 | 8,231 |
| stats | 370 | 513 | 513 |

JSON costs 13-37% more than TOON for identical information; --lean recovers roughly half of that on the two orientation commands and almost none on list/get. Both numbers matter for this item's degradation ladder: the ceiling has to be declared per command, and the encoding choice alone moves a command 13-37% before any content is dropped.

Discovery-surface costs, which have no ceiling at all today:
- `pm --help` 12,281 bytes (77 commands)
- `pm list --help` 6,173 bytes human, 21,941 bytes as `--help --json`
- `pm contracts --summary` 3,598 bytes versus `pm contracts --json` 66,015 bytes

The 18x gap between contracts summary and full contracts is the shape this item wants everywhere: a declared default ceiling with an explicit opt-in to the full payload. It already exists on exactly one surface (pm-vxxm shipped it for contracts), and nowhere else.

A two-call cold start (contracts --summary + next) therefore costs about 15,230 bytes today, roughly 3.8k tokens, before the agent reads a single item body. That is the number pm-ka6d's documented orientation path should be measured against, and the number this item's budgets should reduce.

value.text:
Per-depth output cost for a single item read, measured 2026-07-25 on the live tracker against dist 2026.7.25, using pm get pm-doxj:

  --depth brief       2,241 bytes    (~560 tokens)
  --depth standard   20,290 bytes    (~5,070 tokens)   <- the default
  --depth deep      168,335 bytes    (~42,000 tokens)

The ratio is what matters for a budget contract: standard is 9x brief, and deep is 75x brief. The default sits at roughly 5k tokens for one item because standard includes the full body, and a roadmap or epic body grows without bound over the item's life — pm-doxj's body is a multi-year running document. There is no cap and no truncation notice at any depth, so a single pm get can consume a quarter of a small context window with no signal that it did.

Two consequences for the budgets this item defines. First, a per-command budget expressed as one number cannot describe pm get: its cost is a function of the item, not the command, so the contract needs a per-depth budget plus a body-truncation policy with a disclosed continuation. Second, --depth deep at 42k tokens is beyond any plausible agent budget and should probably carry an explicit warning or require acknowledgement rather than being one flag away from the default.

Related measurement for the same corpus question on pm-z71aoy: these figures come from the real 2,037-item tracker, not from a fixture workspace, and the spread between them is entirely item-data-driven — which is exactly the representativeness failure that item describes.

patch.value:
Every command already declares a default output ceiling in the contracts table, and the declaration binds nothing. It is not enforced at runtime, and it is not the oracle of either gate that carries the word token in its name. The result is a surface where the published number and the delivered number are unrelated.

Conformance census, measured at HEAD build 2026.7.28 against this repository's tracker of 2,154 items and 40,446 history entries, using the contract's own metric of ceil(utf8_bytes / 4):

  command      declared   measured     ratio
  activity        4,000  1,591,219    397.8x
  deps            4,000     46,498     11.6x
  health          6,000     33,178      5.5x
  list            4,000     14,234      3.6x
  duplicates      4,000      9,552      2.4x
  events          4,000      9,199      2.3x
  validate        6,000      5,962      1.0x
  contracts       3,000      2,245      0.7x
  next            4,000      2,201      0.6x
  context         4,000      2,016      0.5x
  get             4,000      1,400      0.3x
  graph           4,000        403      0.1x
  aggregate       4,000        114      0.0x
  stats           6,000        110      0.0x

Seven of eighteen sampled surfaces exceed their declared ceiling; one sits exactly at it. The distribution is the important part: the overruns are not uniform overhead, they are the surfaces whose output size is a function of workspace scale and whose bound is missing rather than loose. A ceiling that a command exceeds by 397.8x on a mid-sized workspace is not a ceiling that grows too slowly, it is a command with no bound at all.

Two consequences shape what this feature has to deliver.

The declared number cannot stay advisory metadata. An agent reading default_max_estimated_tokens today is reading a value that predicts nothing about what the call will cost, which is worse than the value being absent, because absence would at least prompt a bounded call.

Enforcement and measurement have to move together. The corpus gate this feature extends is currently measured against a three-item fixture with self-recorded byte budgets, so it cannot observe a scale-dependent overrun at all; that blindness is owned by pm-9sui7t and is the negative control this feature's fourth criterion needs in order to mean anything.

Individual overruns retain their own owners and are not absorbed here: pm-z2j1qt owns activity, pm-t2t709 owns deps, pm-du93sr owns health, pm-mfy1ux owns graph impact. This item owns the general contract -- that a declared ceiling is binding, that exceeding it degrades deterministically down the published ladder, that the envelope discloses what was dropped, and that an unbounded result must be asked for by name.

value.text:
Measured baseline and degradation-ladder design, 2026-07-28, on the real 2,176-item workspace at HEAD. Recorded here because the budget contract cannot be set without knowing what the current defaults actually cost, and because the shape of the waste is more informative than its size.

MEASURED COST OF THE MANDATED AGENT LOOP. AGENTS.md instructs an agent to orient with four reads before doing any work.

  pm context --limit 10                 7,075 B   about 1,770 tokens
  pm next                               8,603 B   about 2,150 tokens
  pm list-open --limit 20               4,713 B   about 1,180 tokens
  pm search <keywords> --limit 10       3,980 B   about   995 tokens
  total orientation                    24,371 B   about 6,095 tokens

Other agent-facing reads on the same corpus:

  pm get <id>                           7,813 B   about 1,953 tokens
  pm get <id> --fields id,title,status    163 B   about    40 tokens
  pm deps <id>                         63,725 B   about 15,931 tokens
  pm validate                          22,754 B   about 5,688 tokens
  pm contracts --summary                8,645 B   about 2,161 tokens
  pm graph analyze                      1,617 B   about   404 tokens
  pm aggregate --group-by status          457 B   about   114 tokens

THE SHAPE OF THE WASTE. The single largest ratio in the table is not a slow command, it is a default. pm get costs 48 times its projected form for the same item, which means the expensive answer is what an agent gets by asking the obvious question and the cheap answer requires knowing a flag. Every ratio of this kind in the corpus has the same structure - a correct cheap form exists and is not the default - and that is the pattern pm-cxr0jb owns for projections, pm-mfy1ux for graph impact, pm-du93sr for health --check-only, and pm-okgxwa for explain-ranking. The budget contract this item declares is what makes those four stop recurring, because a declared ceiling forces a default to be inside it.

FOUR MECHANISMS, in the order they should land.

One - intent-declared default projections. Each command declares, in contract data, the field set its declared intent consumes, and that set is the default. Widening is explicit. This is pm-cxr0jb and it is the highest-leverage single change in the table, because it converts the 48x get ratio and the per-row cost of every list surface at once. The declaration must be data so that the token gate can compute the expected cost of the default without running it.

Two - reference then dereference. Rows carry stable ids and bounded discriminators; prose bodies, acceptance criteria, and annotation text arrive only when a caller asks to expand. An agent scanning twenty candidates needs to distinguish them, not read them. Today a list row that includes a description pays for prose the agent discards in nineteen of twenty cases. This is the row-contract half of pm-sb0tns and must be decided with it, since it changes what a row IS.

Three - per-response interning. Status, type, author, tag, and parent values repeat across every row of every response, and the id prefix repeats on every id. A response-level dictionary declaring the repeated values once and referring to them positionally is a pure encoding win that changes no semantics and no field set. pm-ez1dfg already measured the extreme case: per-row cursor overhead is 48 to 53 percent of the bytes in pm events. pm-kvxqp1 owns the general encoding study and this is its clearest candidate; it composes with mechanism one rather than competing, because interning shrinks whatever field set survives projection.

Four - answer-shaped output. pm next answers one question - what should I do now - and costs 2,150 tokens to do it. The answer is one id, one reason, and the bounded set of alternatives the caller might override with. pm-cxr0jb covers the projection half; pm-08mt4k covers the correctness half, since the current recommendation can be a milestone gate with no children; and pm-okgxwa covers the explanation being sized by the workspace rather than by the answer. The three together are what makes next cheap, and none of them alone does.

THE DEGRADATION LADDER. A ceiling is only a contract if exceeding it has a declared, deterministic consequence. Proposed ladder, applied in order, each rung declared per command in contract data rather than chosen at runtime:

  rung 0  full answer inside the ceiling, nothing omitted
  rung 1  drop expansion fields, keep every row and every discriminator
  rung 2  reduce row count against the declared ordering, and report the exact number withheld with a resumable cursor
  rung 3  substitute a declared summary shape whose own cost is contracted
  rung 4  refuse with a structured error naming the narrowing flag that would fit

Two properties make the ladder honest and both are currently absent. Every rung must state what it omitted, so an agent never mistakes a truncated answer for a complete one - which is the same requirement pm-q7qojt just closed for the list --all completeness claim. And the rung reached must be reported in the envelope, so the token gate can assert that ordinary corpora reach rung 0 and only pathological ones descend.

WHY THE GATES CANNOT ENFORCE THIS YET. pm-9sui7t is in the current unreleased set precisely because both token gates were structurally unable to fail - one measured only help payloads, the other measured command output against a three-item fixture. pm-z71aoy owns corpus representativeness and pm-dpqa3h owns the orphaned measurement harness. Until a gate measures real output on a real corpus against the declared ceiling, every number in this note is a snapshot rather than an invariant, and the ceilings this item declares will drift the moment they are written.

SCALE INVARIANCE. The ceilings must hold at both ends of the range the product claims. On a five-item workspace the whole corpus is cheaper than most ceilings and every rung must be a no-op, so the ladder must not impose a summary on an answer that already fits. At a million items the ceiling binds on every read and rung 2 becomes the common case, which makes the resumable cursor and the withheld count load-bearing rather than diagnostic. A single set of declared numbers cannot serve both; the ceiling should be declared per command and the ladder parameterised by corpus size, with the parameterisation itself in contract data so it is inspectable rather than emergent. pm-tch9cs is the fleet-level companion: per-command ceilings bound one answer and nothing yet bounds the aggregate the fleet pays.

value.text:
Baseline re-measured 2026-07-29 on the 2,186-item tracker, plus the degradation-receipt requirement the measurements force.

Current cost table. stats 440 bytes, about 110 tokens. health --summary 570, about 142. get pm-doxj --depth brief 3,741, about 935. search with limit 10 is 4,205, about 1,051. list-open with limit 20 is 4,548, about 1,137. context with limit 10 is 7,694, about 1,923. next with limit 5 is 8,575, about 2,143. activity --compact with limit 50 is 10,568, about 2,642. contracts default 11,843, about 2,960. Root help 13,075, about 3,268. All 84 per-command helps together 212,496, about 53,124. activity --full with limit 50 is 671,002, about 167,750. contracts --full is 1,142,247, about 285,561.

Orientation is cheaper than it was. context plus next plus list-open is now 20,817 bytes, about 5,203 tokens, against the roughly 6,095 tokens recorded earlier under this item. The contracts entry point in particular fell from 125,193 bytes to 11,843, a factor of 10.6, because the summary shape is now the default. That improvement is real and should be stated as such rather than re-litigated.

The spread is the ungoverned quantity. Cheapest useful command 110 tokens, most expensive shape 285,561 tokens. That is a factor of 2,596 across one product with no declared policy anywhere in between. Worse, the ratio between shapes of a single command is also ungoverned and is large: activity compact to full is 63.5x, health summary to plain is 233x on the earlier measurement, graph impact summary to default is 1,029x, contracts default to full is 96x. A budget contract that declares only a per-command ceiling does not constrain this ratio, and the ratio is precisely what decides whether an agent that picks the wrong shape survives.

The observation that makes the ladder design harder than it looks. In every one of those pairs the expensive shape is the only one that carries the answer. activity --full is the only projection that carries agent provenance. contracts --full is the only complete declared surface. health plain is the only shape with the extensions detail. The cheap shape is cheap because it omits the thing that was asked for. So a degradation ladder cannot be specified as cheap-by-default with an escape hatch; it has to be specified as a sequence of shapes each of which states what it dropped.

Degradation receipts today, four commands and four different answers. pm list declares a projection object naming its mode and the exact fields it emitted. pm context declares sections_included and names them honestly, empty at brief, six names at standard, ten at deep. pm activity declares only the boolean compact, with no field list. pm get declares nothing at all: at brief depth its envelope is empty and it silently drops children, claim_state and linked, which are present at standard. pm search carries no projection key of any kind.

And all four of the ones that do declare something name what is present, never what is absent. That is the wrong polarity for a budget contract. An agent deciding whether to spend more needs to know what it would gain, which is the complement, and it can only compute the complement if it already knows the full field set, which is what it was trying to avoid loading. The receipt must name the omission and the price of retrieving it.

The requirement this adds to the item. Every bounded read shape emits an omission receipt: which named field groups or sections were withheld, and the flag that would restore each. Row omission already works this way, with a count, a has_more and a resumable cursor, so the pattern exists in the product and only needs extending from rows to fields. A shape that withholds nothing says so explicitly rather than omitting the receipt, because an absent receipt and a complete payload must not look alike.

A second requirement follows for the top of the ladder. A complete surface that no consumer can load is indistinguishable from an absent one. contracts --full at 285,561 tokens has never been read by any agent and never will be. The full form should be paged or queryable against the same predicate grammar as the rest of the product rather than emitted whole, and the ceiling contract should forbid any shape whose declared budget exceeds a working context window without a paging affordance.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Bounding-surface census 2026-07-30 (evening) at HEAD, recorded here because this item owns the ceiling contract and the census is the shape the contract has to govern.

Seventeen distinct output-bounding flag spellings exist across twenty read commands, and no two commands expose the same set: --after, --brief, --check-only, --depth, --fields, --for, --format, --full, --limit, --max-items, --no-truncate, --sample-limit, --section, --stream, --summary, --token-budget, --blocked-limit. Per command: the four list variants nine each, context eight, search six, get five, next five, deps four, graph four, health four, history three, activity three, events two, contracts two, comments one, notes one, validate one, and files, stats and aggregate zero.

Three findings for the contract.

The budget flag is on three of twenty and it is on the wrong three. next, context and deps declare --token-budget. list, get and search declare intent budgets, enforce them at egress and reject the flag outright, so a caller who hits a ceiling on those three has no override. This is reachable today: pm list --limit 200 --for triage and pm get <id> --depth deep --for inspect both return a receipt with zero rows and no way to raise the limit.

The declared ceilings themselves are not reachable on this corpus for three of five intents, measured floors against declared budgets: next execute 1,438 against 1200, context orient 8,417 against 2400, context handoff the same. All five fit on a two-item workspace. A ceiling contract therefore needs a reachability clause, not only an enforcement clause.

Bounded is not the same as cheap. Walking all 315 open items through the triage intent costs 158 pages at 6,250 bytes each, roughly 987,500 bytes, against 71,709 bytes for the single unprojected call, because eight chain-invariant metadata blocks are re-emitted on a two-row page. Per row that is 3,125 bytes against 228. The ceiling contract should state the cost of a full walk, not only the cost of a page, or it will keep certifying payloads that are individually small and collectively 13.8 times larger than the form they replaced.

The two issues that carry the fixes are filed under this item, and the receipt accounting question this item already tracked is unchanged: the receipts now report 5.4 to 5.6 emitted bytes per estimated token, so the estimator remains optimistic against real serialised output.

value.text: Evidence measured 2026-08-07. `pm deps <id>` carries an undeclared default ceiling of 16,000 estimated tokens — the largest default in the surface, roughly three times the whole documented agent cold start — enforced by a private vocabulary (--token-budget, --node-limit, --edge-limit, --max-depth) rather than the universal read controls. On this workspace it truncates 1,341 of 1,381 nodes and 6,645 of 6,694 edges to stay under it, and the number appears in no help text, no contract summary, and no doc. Separately `pm contracts --full --json` emits 389,951 estimated tokens with no default ceiling at all. Both are the same gap this item closes: a ceiling that exists but is not contracted is indistinguishable from no ceiling to the agent that has to plan around it.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Measured 2026-08-13 on the live tracker: the ceiling this item asks for exists and is opt-in, so the default path is unbounded.

pm list-open --limit 1 --full  -> 365,315 bytes (~91,300 tokens)
pm list-open --limit 2 --full  -> 378,848 bytes
pm list-open --limit 5 --full  -> 619,662 bytes
pm list-open --limit 10 --full -> 922,471 bytes
pm list-open --limit 20 --full -> 994,450 bytes (~248,600 tokens)

One row can exceed 90,000 tokens because --full inlines unbounded child collections verbatim. Field sizes for the largest single row: notes 318,223 bytes, comments 36,617, dependencies 2,661, learnings 717. The row's own scalar fields total under 1,200 bytes, so 99.7 percent of the payload is collections whose size no flag on the invocation bounds.

The bound already works when asked for: pm list-open --limit 20 --full --token-budget 2000 returns 792 bytes. So the degradation machinery this item specifies is built and correct; what is missing is that no default ceiling applies it. A documented projection flag can therefore emit a payload two to three times larger than a frontier agent's entire context window, and nothing in the invocation, the help text or the response warns before it happens.

Two further observations for the design. First, the per-row cost is not monotone in --limit: limit 1 costs 365 KB and limit 20 costs 994 KB, so cost tracks which items are in the window rather than how many, which means a per-row estimate cannot be derived from the limit and the ceiling has to be enforced during assembly. Second, --brief and the default projection on list-open are byte-identical (both report projection mode 'brief'), so the flag documented as the agent-optimized token saver saves nothing on the most common read; the saving is real only against --compact and --full.
